description: Width tiers for English Year 6 — all 23 descriptors. One width_entry per descriptor code.
subject: English

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor that satisfies the descriptor's command term. For concept/understanding standards (LA, LE, texts in context): the fewest contexts or phenomena that genuinely meet the command term. For capability standards (Mode B Literacy): the simplest context in which the capability is demonstrably performed.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope grounded in the most common elaboration cases. What a well-taught Year 6 class engaging fully with the descriptor would have done.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new contexts, phenomena, cultural perspectives or task types — not harder versions of the same context. First Nations Australian directions included where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA v9 elaborations are the primary source data. They are treated as examples of how the descriptor might be addressed, not as a required sequence. Wider may infer beyond elaborations where the direction is clearly within the descriptor's scope and year band.

AC9E6LA01.minimum_width: Identify and discuss three points on the formality continuum (e.g. slang, conversational, formal) using provided examples; explain one feature that signals each register level.
AC9E6LA01.typical_width: Discuss and sort spoken and written examples across the full formality continuum; explain how vocabulary, sentence structure and tone signal register; explain how social distance (familiarity and power relationship) determines appropriate register for a range of contexts including peer, teacher, community leader and ceremonial situations.
wider: Compare the same message expressed across all four register levels and analyse how meaning and relationship signal shift across the continuum
Examine how digital communication creates new hybrid registers that blend formal and informal features and discuss what social distance signals these carry
Investigate how formal address protocols differ across institutions (school, government, royalty) and what social values they encode
Compare how formality and social distance are linguistically marked in other languages with formal pronoun systems and discuss what this reveals about language and social structure
elaborations: recognising language protocols for formal address; for example, words used to address principals, heads of state and monarchs
discussing levels of language such as slang, colloquial, conversational and formal, and how their appropriateness changes with the situation and audience
presenting ideas and opinions at levels of formality appropriate to the context and audience

AC9E6LA02.minimum_width: Identify and distinguish at least two objective sentences and two subjective sentences in provided texts; identify one emotive or judgement word in a persuasive text and explain its positioning effect.
AC9E6LA02.typical_width: Analyse how objective and subjective language function across multiple text types (factual recounts, personal recounts, editorials, reviews, advertisements); explain how emotive vocabulary and judgement words evoke emotion and persuade audiences; explain the distinction between reporting facts and providing commentary; identify at least one example of bias in a text and explain how language choices construct it.
wider: Compare a factual news report and an editorial on the same event, annotating the shift from objective to subjective language and analysing what the shift reveals about each text's purpose
Analyse how the same event or product is described using different emotive language for different target audiences
Compare how unedited vs. captioned or cropped photographs of the same event can construct different perspectives
Examine bias across two news sources covering the same story and evaluate how language choices advantage different perspectives
elaborations: identifying language choices that evoke emotion and judgements in direct and indirect ways, and how they are used to persuade different audiences to take a position and/or action
understanding when to share feelings and opinions; for example, in a personal recount, and when to remain more objective; for example, in a factual recount
differentiating between reporting the facts; for example, in a factual recount or unedited photograph, and providing a commentary; for example, in an editorial

AC9E6LA03.minimum_width: Identify the stages of one familiar text type and name at least one phase within a stage; identify one example where an author has adapted a typical structural feature and explain the effect.
AC9E6LA03.typical_width: Explain the characteristic stages and phases of multiple text types — narrative, review, discussion of alternative positions, historical recount; identify and explain when and why authors adapt typical text structures or language features; analyse at least two examples of structural adaptation across different text types.
wider: Explore a range of everyday, community, literary and informative texts, comparing overall structure and the effect of authors' choices across at least two texts
Examine how humour texts use structural features differently — for example, how exaggeration functions within a structural stage
Analyse how reviews, discussions and historical recounts each have characteristic stages and identify any adaptations in provided examples
Map the stage and phase structure of a film or picture book narrative and compare visual and written structural signals
elaborations: exploring a range of everyday, community, literary and informative texts, discussing elements of text structure and language features, and comparing the overall structure and effect of authors' choices in 2 or more texts
examining a text to identify strategies such as exaggeration to create humour

recognising that texts are organised into stages such as an introduction and that introductions may be divided into phases; for example, the introduction stage of a narrative may begin with a phase that is a "hook" or a flashback
explaining the characteristic stages and phases in reviews, discussions of alternative positions or historical recounts and identifying any adaptations of typical structures or language features

AC9E6LA04.minimum_width: Identify at least two cohesive links created by key word repetition or synonyms; identify one example of general-for-specific word association and explain the cohesive link it creates.
AC9E6LA04.typical_width: Recognise and explain how cohesion is built through key word repetition, synonyms, antonyms and word associations across a range of text types; explain how threading these language choices holds a text together thematically.
wider: Analyse how repetition functions differently in literary texts (for effect and aesthetic purpose) vs. informational texts (for clarity and coherence)
Examine a speech or persuasive text where repetition is used structurally (e.g. anaphora) and explain its rhetorical effect beyond basic cohesion
Write a short informative paragraph that deliberately uses word associations and synonyms, then annotate the cohesive devices used
elaborations: noting how a general word is often used for a more specific word already mentioned (word association); for example, "Look at those apples. Granny Smiths are my favourite."
recognising how cohesion can be developed through repeating key words or by using synonyms or antonyms

AC9E6LA05.minimum_width: Identify embedded clauses in at least two provided sentences and explain how an embedded clause is positioned differently from a trailing dependent clause; construct one sentence with an embedded clause and name the noun group it expands.
AC9E6LA05.typical_width: Identify and explain embedded clauses across a range of sentence types; distinguish them from adverbial dependent clauses; construct complex sentences with embedded clauses to elaborate, extend and explain ideas; select appropriate conjunctions.
wider: Analyse a paragraph from a curriculum-area text and identify where embedded clauses are used and what noun groups they expand
Experiment with stacking multiple clauses and evaluate where embedded clauses create clarity vs. awkwardness
Edit a piece of own writing to introduce embedded clauses where they add precision, and reflect on the effect
Compare the effect of an embedded clause vs. a trailing clause conveying the same information
AC9E6LA05.width_notes: Limited width for the identification node — the concept does not vary across contexts. Production and editing contexts (own writing, curriculum-area texts) provide the meaningful width for the construction node.
elaborations: investigating how the choice of conjunctions enables the construction of complex sentences to extend, to elaborate on and to explain ideas; for example, "The town that was flooded suffered extensive damage."
creating complex sentences with embedded clauses to expand noun groups; for example, "Hamish studied the rock samples that he had collected on the excursion."

AC9E6LA06.minimum_width: Replace at least two general verbs with more precise alternatives and explain the meaning change; identify the difference between simple present for a present state vs. a habitual action in two provided sentences; identify and classify one adverb group by type.
AC9E6LA06.typical_width: Analyse how precise verb choices sharpen meaning across different text types; understand and use the three functions of simple present tense (present state, habitual action, timeless truth) and at least three ways of expressing future time; use adverb groups to add precision about manner, place, time or degree in writing.
wider: Compare verb choices in two information reports on the same topic and analyse how verb precision affects authority and clarity
Examine verbs of saying in narratives and explain what each adds beyond the neutral 'said'
Analyse how tense choices function across information reports, narratives and procedure texts and explain why different text types use different tense conventions
Edit a piece of own writing to evaluate whether each adverb group adds necessary precision or is redundant given precise verb choices
elaborations: knowing that the simple present tense is typically used to talk about present states; for example, "He lives in Darwin." or actions that happen regularly in the present; for example, "He watches television every night." or that represent "timeless" happenings, in information reports; for example, "Bears hibernate in winter."

knowing that there are various ways in English to refer to future time: using the auxiliary "will"; for example, "She will call you tomorrow.", using the present tense; for example, "Tomorrow, I leave for Hobart." and using adverbials of time; for example, "She arrives in the morning."
using precise verbs; for example, "slice", "dice", "fillet" and "segment" rather than general words; for example, "cut"

AC9E6LA07.minimum_width: Explain how one sequential visual representation (e.g. flowchart) and one conceptual visual (e.g. table or graph) contribute to meaning; explain why some images and maps may be culturally sensitive for First Nations Australians.
AC9E6LA07.typical_width: Identify and explain how the full range of visual representations (images, figures, tables, diagrams, maps, graphs, flowcharts, timelines, photo stories, life-cycle diagrams) contribute to meaning across different text types; discuss cultural sensitivity and appropriateness when using images and maps relating to First Nations Australians.
wider: Compare the same data presented as a table and a graph and evaluate which is more effective for different reading purposes
Analyse a map from a curriculum-area text (geography, history) and explain how design choices (scale, symbols, orientation) affect meaning
Research how First Nations Australian communities manage the use and sharing of culturally significant images and maps and compare with general copyright practices
Create a visual representation for a curriculum-area process and evaluate whether it communicates more efficiently than prose
elaborations: observing how sequential events can be represented visually by a series of images, including comic strips, timelines, photo stories, procedure diagrams and flowcharts, life-cycle diagrams and the flow of images in picture books
observing how concepts, information and relationships can be represented visually through tables, maps, graphs and diagrams
understanding that images and maps may be sensitive for First Nations Australians and ensuring that a disclaimer is applied or judgement is used about cultural appropriateness and sensitivities

AC9E6LA08.minimum_width: Identify and correctly name at least three figurative language device types in provided texts; explain the literal vs. figurative meaning of one example; use at least two figurative language terms accurately in a written or spoken response.
AC9E6LA08.typical_width: Identify and name all six device types (metaphor, simile, personification, idiom, imagery, hyperbole) in a range of texts; explain how figurative language creates vivid and less predictable meanings compared with literal vocabulary; use subject metalanguage (device names) fluently and accurately when discussing texts; explain how idioms have fixed non-literal meanings.
wider: Research the origins of several common English idioms and explain how literal meanings relate to figurative use
Compare figurative language use in texts by First Nations Australian authors — identifying imagery and language choices and discussing how they create meaning
Analyse how figurative language choices in a poem create an extended or sustained impression rather than isolated effects
Analyse figurative language in a persuasive text (e.g. a review) and explain how it shapes the reader's emotional response
elaborations: exploring how figurative language; for example, metaphors, personification and idioms, can be used to create vivid and less predictable shades of meaning
identifying authors' use of vivid and emotive vocabulary in persuasive texts; for example, the vocabulary used in reviews
discussing texts, using vocabulary to name text structure, literary devices and language features; for example, using words that name the literary device used in a poem

AC9E6LA09.minimum_width: Identify which of the three comma uses applies in at least four provided sentences; explain the rule for each use in own words; produce one sentence demonstrating each use correctly.
AC9E6LA09.typical_width: Identify and explain all three comma uses across a range of sentences including compound sentences; use commas accurately across all three purposes in extended writing including dialogue.
wider: Analyse a professional writer's use of commas in a passage and classify each use, noting any uses beyond the three taught
Research the Oxford comma debate and form a reasoned opinion about whether it should be used
Edit a provided passage with comma errors, correct them and explain each correction
AC9E6LA09.width_notes: Limited width — comma rules are relatively narrow in scope. Wider directions focus on meta-level analysis of conventions and professional usage rather than additional contexts for the same rules.
elaborations: identifying different uses of commas such as commas and conjunctions between independent clauses in compound sentences
using commas in dialogue; for example, Ben said, "I want pie, peas, carrots and chips for dinner, followed by ice cream for dessert, please."

AC9E6LE01.minimum_width: Identify and describe the context (historical, social, or cultural) of at least one text by a First Nations Australian or world author; explain at least one way the context shapes responses to a character or event.
AC9E6LE01.typical_width: Read and respond to texts by First Nations Australian, wide-ranging Australian and world authors; discuss how historical, social and cultural experiences may influence responses to characters, actions and events; explain how both text context and reader context shape response; explore how heroes are portrayed across science fiction, fantasy and realistic settings.
wider: Compare responses to the same character from a contemporary reader and a reader from the text's historical context
Examine how heroes are portrayed in science fiction or fantasy vs. more realistic settings from texts by First Nations Australian and world authors
Explore reviews of Australian films and identify how reviewers interpret cultural contexts in their responses
Compare how two authors from different cultural backgrounds represent a shared theme (e.g. belonging, courage) and analyse similarities and differences
elaborations: discussing the influence historical, social and cultural experiences may have on the meaning of a text and attitudes towards characters, actions and events
sharing responses about how heroes are portrayed in science fiction or fantasy and more realistic settings
exploring reviews of Australian films

AC9E6LE02.minimum_width: Identify at least one similarity and one difference in structural features, and one similarity and one difference in language or visual features, between two texts on a similar topic or theme.
AC9E6LE02.typical_width: Compare at least two texts on similar topics, themes or plots; identify differences in narrator, narrative structure, voice, and language and visual features; explain how these differences influence how readers or viewers interpret the topic or theme.
wider: Compare two fantasy quest novels or two realistic novels on a specific theme from different authors or cultural contexts
Compare texts on the same theme with very different styles (e.g. picture book and chapter book) to identify what stylistic differences produce different reader experiences
Analyse how the choice of first-person vs. third-person narrator shapes reader identification across two texts on the same theme
elaborations: exploring texts on a similar topic by authors with very different styles; for example, comparing fantasy quest novels or realistic novels on a specific theme
identifying differences in the use of narrator, narrative structure and voice, and language and visual features, between texts and determining how these influence readers or viewers

AC9E6LE03.minimum_width: Identify at least two characteristics that appear across two or more texts by the same author; explain these as defining features of the author's style rather than features of a single text.
AC9E6LE03.typical_width: Explore two or more texts by the same author; identify characteristic elements including subject, theme, characterisation, text structure, plot development, tone, vocabulary, voice, grammatical structures, and visual techniques; produce an explanation of the author's individual style using textual evidence.
wider: Focus on a First Nations Australian author and identify characteristic elements of their writing including images, themes and language choices
Compare illustrations across picture books by the same illustrator and identify the characteristic visual features that define their style
Compare the defining style features of two authors in the same genre and explain what makes each distinctive
Write a short piece in the style of a chosen author and annotate the choices made to reflect identified style elements
elaborations: exploring 2 or more texts by the same author, identifying similarities; for example, subject or theme, characterisation, text structure, plot development, tone, vocabulary, voice, favoured grammatical structures and visual techniques in picture books, and determining the qualities that characterise an author's style
focusing on a First Nations Australian author and identifying characteristic elements of their writing; for example, images, theme and language

comparing similarities and differences between texts, including those by the same author or illustrator, and identifying the characteristics that define an author's style; for example, comparing illustrations in picture books by the same illustrator, noting characteristic features

AC9E6LE04.minimum_width: Identify and name alliteration, assonance and onomatopoeia in provided poems; identify at least one image in a poem and explain how it creates emotional engagement; identify a regular rhythmic pattern in a ballad and explain one effect.
AC9E6LE04.typical_width: Describe the effects of alliteration, assonance and onomatopoeia; explain how imagery builds emotional connections and engagement in poetry; explain the effect of rhythm in ballads and its relationship to oral tradition; analyse a poem identifying how sound devices and imagery work together to create meaning and effect.
wider: Identify the imagery used in narratives or poetry about First Nations Australians' Country/Place and discuss how it reflects relationships between people, land and story
Compare how an Australian poem and a poem from another cultural context use sound and imagery to convey a theme
Analyse how multiple sound devices work together in the same poem to create a cumulative effect
Write a short poem that deliberately employs at least two sound devices and one sustained image, then annotate the choices
elaborations: explaining how imagery builds emotional connections and engagement with the story or theme
identifying the imagery used in narratives or poetry about First Nations Australians' Country/Place
describing the effects of assonance, alliteration and onomatopoeia in a poem
explaining the effect of rhythm in ballads

AC9E6LE05.minimum_width: Create a short literary text (written, spoken or multimodal) that adapts at least one element from a source text (e.g. reimagining the hero); use at least one literary device; make at least one edit against a stated criterion.
AC9E6LE05.typical_width: Create and edit a literary text that adapts multiple elements (plot structure, characters, settings and/or ideas) from a text experienced; experiment with literary devices; discuss setting choices with a peer during editing; explain editing choices; produce in written, spoken or multimodal/digital form.
wider: Create an autobiography of a character from a text explored, inferring from the source while adding a new interpretive layer
Create a literary text adapting from a First Nations Australian text, engaging respectfully with cultural elements and explaining choices made
Create an adaptation that deliberately shifts the cultural or social context of the source text and present with an author's note explaining the rationale
Discuss the setting in a literary text with a peer during editing and experiment with literary devices that enhance the setting
elaborations: creating narratives in written, spoken or multimodal/digital form adapting character; for example, reimagining the hero in an adventure story
creating an autobiography of a character from a text explored
discussing the setting in a literary text with a peer during the editing process, and experimenting with literary devices that may enhance the setting

AC9E6LY01.minimum_width: Identify at least one feature of a provided text (including a media text) that reflects the context of its creation; explain why a text from a different context might represent the same event or idea differently.
AC9E6LY01.typical_width: Examine and compare texts including media texts (news reports, advertisements, film promotions) from different contexts; identify how representations of ideas and events reflect their contexts of creation; explain the impact of context-shaped representation choices on audience expectations.
wider: Identify news reports of the same type of event over time and analyse how the reports reflect their historical contexts
Compare advertising posters for animated children's films in different countries and explain how cultural context shapes audience expectations
Identify how advertisements for the same products reflect the contexts in which they were created
Examine how the same news story is represented in two different media outlets and identify how institutional context shapes the representation
elaborations: identifying news reports of the same type of event over time and how they reflect their contexts
comparing advertising posters for animated children's films in different countries and explaining the impact of these choices on audience expectations of the film
identifying how advertisements for the same products reflect the context in which they were created

AC9E6LY02.minimum_width: Participate in a discussion demonstrating at least two interaction strategies (e.g. paraphrasing and asking a clarifying question); use language that matches the formality level of the context.
AC9E6LY02.typical_width: Participate in pair, group, class, school and community speaking and listening situations including informal conversations, discussions, debates and formal presentations; use the full range of interaction strategies (pausing, questioning, rephrasing, repeating, summarising, reviewing); adjust formality appropriately; develop and support at least one argument orally.
wider: Participate in a formal debate or structured academic discussion and reflect on how the format shaped argument development
Lead a structured group discussion ensuring all participants contribute and arguments are developed and evaluated
Analyse a transcript of a formal vs. informal spoken exchange and identify the specific features that signal each context
Recognise that open questions prompt elaboration while closed questions ask for precise responses — and practise using both strategically
elaborations: participating in pair, group, class, school and community speaking and listening situations, including informal conversations, discussions, debates and presentations
using strategies; for example, pausing, questioning, rephrasing, repeating, summarising, reviewing and asking clarifying questions when discussing topics
recognising that closed questions ask for precise responses while open questions prompt a speaker to provide more information

AC9E6LY03.minimum_width: Identify at least one structural feature and one language feature in a text and explain how both contribute to the same purpose; identify at least one choice designed to engage or influence the audience and explain the effect.
AC9E6LY03.typical_width: Analyse how text structures and language features work together as a system to meet the purpose of a text; compare print and digital sources on similar topics and evaluate which features best aid navigation and clear communication; explain how specific choices engage and influence audiences.
wider: Compare the structural and language feature combinations in two texts with the same purpose and evaluate which combination is more effective for the intended audience
Analyse a multimodal text and explain how layout, image and written language features work together to serve purpose and engage audience
elaborations: comparing the structure and language features of different texts, including print and digital sources on similar topics, and evaluating which features best aid navigation and clear communication about the topic

AC9E6LY04.minimum_width: Use at least two structural features to locate specific information in a text for a stated purpose; evaluate the effectiveness of at least one structural feature and explain whether it aids navigation.
AC9E6LY04.typical_width: Use knowledge of text structure to navigate a range of print and digital texts using the full range of structural features (table of contents, glossary, chapters, headings, subheadings); evaluate how features serve navigation and comprehension; select and evaluate texts for a research task; apply research skills — locating, gathering and organising information.
wider: Compare navigation features in a print vs. digital text on the same topic and evaluate which better serves a specific reading purpose
Compare structural feature use across curriculum-area texts (science textbook, geography atlas) and explain what each subject's conventions reveal about how readers use those texts
Design an improved structural feature for a provided text and explain how it better serves the reader
Evaluate a digital source for credibility indicators (author, publication, date, evidence) and explain the reasoning
elaborations: bringing subject and technical vocabulary and concept knowledge to new reading tasks, selecting, evaluating and using texts for their pertinence to the task and the accuracy of their information
using knowledge of text structure to navigate the text to locate specific literal content for a purpose
using research skills including locating texts, gathering and organising information, evaluating and using information

AC9E6LY05.minimum_width: Apply at least two comprehension strategies to extract literal meaning from a text; make at least one inference and name the textual evidence that supports it.
AC9E6LY05.typical_width: Use the full range of comprehension strategies (visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, monitoring, questioning) to build literal and inferred meaning; connect information in print and images; use graphic organisers to visualise connections, categories and hierarchies; connect and compare content from at least two sources.
wider: Apply comprehension strategies to a complex multimodal text and evaluate which strategies were most useful for different types of information
Compare inferences made by different readers of the same text and discuss what prior knowledge or experience shaped different interpretations
Investigate a topic using sources from different disciplines (e.g. science article, historical account, First Nations knowledge source) and compare what each perspective reveals
Compare the claims of three or more sources on the same topic and evaluate which is best supported by evidence
elaborations: making connections between the text and students' own experience or other texts
making connections between information in print and images
using prior knowledge and textual information to make inferences
asking and answering questions
using graphic organisers to visualise connections, categories and hierarchies of information
summarising a text or part of a text

AC9E6LY06.minimum_width: Plan a text identifying purpose, audience and structure; produce a paragraph including at least one embedded clause and one precise verb choice; make at least two edits against a stated criterion and explain one editing choice.
AC9E6LY06.typical_width: Plan, create, edit and publish texts across imaginative, informative and persuasive purposes using paragraphs, complex sentences including embedded clauses, expanded verb groups, appropriate tense, topic-specific and vivid vocabulary, correct punctuation and spelling, and visual features; use rhetorical devices, images and modal verbs for persuasive effects.
wider: Create informative texts for two different audiences exploring the same topic and note the language changes required for each
Use rhetorical devices, images and modal verbs for persuasive effects for an identified audience
Select and combine digital tools to create a multimodal text and evaluate how visual and written elements work together
Re-read and edit own and others' work using negotiated criteria, explaining editing choices including why specific changes improve meaning, accuracy or impact
elaborations: creating informative texts for 2 different audiences that explore a topic using text structure and language features for the identified audiences, noting the changes required to appeal to each audience
using rhetorical devices, images and modal verbs for persuasive effects, for an identified audience
selecting and combining digital tools to create texts
re-reading and editing their own and others' work using negotiated criteria for text structure, meaning and accuracy of grammar, spelling and punctuation, and explaining editing choices as required

AC9E6LY07.minimum_width: Plan and deliver a spoken or multimodal presentation with at least three logically organised points developing a theme; demonstrate at least two deliberate voice delivery choices; use at least one piece of precise topic vocabulary.
AC9E6LY07.typical_width: Plan, create, rehearse and deliver spoken and multimodal presentations that develop a theme or idea with information, arguments and details; organise ideas using precise topic-specific and technical vocabulary; apply deliberate pitch, tone, pace and volume choices; integrate visual and digital features.
wider: Plan a report on a topic, sequencing ideas logically with supporting detail and graphics/sound/visuals to enhance audience engagement
Present an argument on a learning area content issue with claims supported by evidence, topic vocabulary, and audience-appropriate persuasive techniques
Set goals for a presentation and monitor development in a written or digital journal; evaluate the presentation against those goals after delivery
Record and review own delivery, identifying where voice features supported or undermined the presentation
elaborations: planning a report on a topic, sequencing ideas logically and providing supporting detail, including graphics, sound and visuals to enhance audience engagement and understanding
experimenting with voice effects such as tone, volume, pitch and pace in formal presentations and recognising the effects these have on audience understanding

presenting an argument about an issue from learning area content, which includes claims supported with evidence and examples, careful use of topic-specific vocabulary and selection of persuasive techniques appropriate to audience
setting goals for a presentation and monitoring development in a written or digital journal

AC9E6LY08.minimum_width: Correctly read and spell at least two words with uncommon letter patterns; identify the less common grapheme–phoneme relationship in at least one example.
AC9E6LY08.typical_width: Apply phonic generalisations to read and write complex words with common and uncommon letter patterns; use phonics knowledge to attempt unfamiliar technical and scientific vocabulary encountered in curriculum-area reading.
wider: Apply phonic knowledge to decode unfamiliar subject-specific vocabulary across curriculum areas and explain the strategy used
Research the etymology of words with uncommon letter patterns (e.g. silent 'p' in Greek-derived words) and explain how knowing origins aids phonic decoding
Collect examples of uncommon letter patterns from curriculum-area reading and identify the grapheme–phoneme pattern each represents
AC9E6LY08.width_notes: Limited width — the concept of grapheme–phoneme relationships does not vary meaningfully across contexts at this year band. Wider directions focus on applying phonic knowledge to new vocabulary domains (curriculum areas) and connecting phonic patterns to etymology.
elaborations: using phonic generalisations to read and write complex words with uncommon letter patterns; for example, "pneumonia", "resuscitate" and "vegetation"

AC9E6LY09.minimum_width: Identify the Greek or Latin root in at least two provided words and explain how root knowledge helps with spelling and meaning; identify a prefix or suffix in at least two words and explain the meaning change; correctly spell at least three words applying a spelling generalisation.
AC9E6LY09.typical_width: Use knowledge of word origins (Latin and Greek roots), base words, prefixes, suffixes, letter patterns and spelling generalisations to spell a range of new words including technical words; use a dictionary to explore word origins; apply morphemic knowledge to spell technical vocabulary from curriculum areas.
wider: Use a dictionary to explore Greek roots (e.g. 'ath', 'pent', 'dec') and generate word families, explaining meaning connections
Investigate the meanings of words in languages of First Nations Australians using dictionaries or online resources from state libraries or universities
Apply accumulated knowledge of a wide range of letter patterns and generalisations to spell new words; for example, 'ratio', 'synthesis', 'reliability', 'handkerchief', 'receive'
Apply morphemic knowledge to spell technical words from curriculum areas (e.g. 'metaphorical', 'biology', 'biodegradable') and explain the morphemic components
elaborations: using a dictionary to explore and using knowledge of word origins, including some Greek roots, to spell words; for example, the Greek root "ath" meaning "contest" or "outstanding skill", "pent" meaning the number 5 and "dec" meaning the number 10 inform the spelling and meaning of the words "athlete", "pentathlon" and "decathlon"
applying accumulated knowledge of a wide range of letter patterns and spelling generalisations to spell new words; for example, "ratio" and "synthesis"
expanding knowledge of prefixes and suffixes, and exploring meaning relationships between words; for example, "disappearance", "submarine", "subterranean", "poisonous" and "nervous"

applying accumulated knowledge of a wide range of letter patterns and spelling generalisations to spell new words; for example, knowing how and why these words are spelt as follows: "reliability", "handkerchief", "receive", "lollies", "trolleys", "climbing", "designed" and "emergency"
spelling technical words by applying morphemic knowledge; for example, "metaphorical", "biology" and "biodegradable"
investigating the meanings of words in languages of First Nations Australians using dictionaries or online resources from state libraries or universities
